newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi says sanctions destroying peace hopes.
newsitem.headline: Burundi says sanctions destroying peace hopes.

text.p: Burundi's military regime reacted angrily on Saturday to a regional summit's decision to maintain economic sanctions on the central African state.
It accused African leaders of undermining peace and having a "secret agenda".

"The government of Burundi expresses its great disappointment following this bad decision which gravely compromises the chances of peace and reconciliation," Information Minister Pierre-Claver Ndayicariye said in a statement broadcast on state radio.
"It seems increasingly clear that in some quarters the objectives are different to those publicly expressed and amount to a secret agenda," the statement said.

Saturday's summit in Arusha, Tanzania, maintained a 10-week embargo and gave a one-month deadline for the start of unconditional peace talks between Major Pierre Buyoya's regime and rebels of Burundi's Hutu majority led by Leonard Nyangoma.
It threatened unspecified further measures if the talks did not begin by November 12.
Buyoya was not invited to the summit but had appealed for an easing or lifting of tough economic sanctions imposed six days after the coup on July 25 by the mainly Tutsi army.
His regime's statement, several hours after news of the intransigent stance at Arusha reached Burundi, made no comment about the order for talks with the rebels.
But it "reiterated the government's commitment to peace" and said the embargo was unjust and a violation of international law.

"It represents a significant encouragement for the criminal actions of terrorist groups who, since the imposition of sanctions, have murdered innocent civilians on the country's roads and hillsides with renewed ardour," the statement said.
The army said earlier on Saturday that Nyangoma's Forces for the Defence of Democracy (FDD) massacred 40 peasants, both Hutu and Tutsi, in villages in Bururi province south of the capital on Friday.
The government called on Burundians to remain calm despite the summit's decision.

The reference to a "secret agenda" underlined the view of many Tutsis that some pro-sanctions nations, particularly Tanzania, favour rule in Burundi by the large Hutu majority which has traditionally played second fiddle to Tutsis.
Many Tutsis oppose talks with Nyangoma, whom they consider a Hutu extremist bent on exterminating the minority.
"A lot of Tutsis will be unhappy," a senior foreign aid official said. "But Buyoya can't afford to let protests get out of hand."
Buyoya banned all political demonstrations after he took power.
